title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a wandering singer with a one-stringed instrument asks where the bird in the cage comes from

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams in one priest, Ramakrishna, who saw the Mother in a cat. Did you feed something hungry as carefully as an offering? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

One string, one note, over and over. On a train platform in rural Bengal, or at a village fair, a singer in a patched saffron robe, hair tied up, holds an instrument with a single string stretched over a gourd, plucks it, and starts to sing. The song is a riddle. There's a strange bird inside the cage, he sings, and I can't tell how it comes and goes. If I could catch it, I'd tie it with the chains of my mind. People stop to listen. Today, our last day in Bengal: the wandering singers called Bauls.
screen: `A SINGER WITH ONE STRING.` → `A BIRD IN THE CAGE.` → `HOW DOES IT COME AND GO?`

segments.voice: The song in the hook, in paraphrase, belongs to Lalon, a Baul singer remembered for songs like this one. The cage is the body. The bird is something living inside it that the singer can feel but can't see or hold. Turn it once. In songs like this one, God isn't looked for mainly in temples or in books. The Bauls sing about the moner manush, the person of the heart: the one you're looking for is already inside you, closer than your own breath, and you keep missing him. That's why the songs are riddles. You can't point straight at something that close. Turn it again, because the Bauls show you where Bengal's streams run into each other. Some of their songs borrow the love of Radha and Krishna from the Vaishnava stream, and some readers hear Sufi Muslim devotion in them too. Lalon himself, in another song, says, in paraphrase: everyone asks what Lalon's caste is, and Lalon says he's never seen what caste looks like. Some wear one kind of prayer beads and some another, he sings, and so people say they're different. The singer won't stand inside the lines people draw. And once more, looking back on these six days. A conch and a drum in one village. Ramprasad talking to Kali like a cross child. Chaitanya singing humbler than grass. Durga coming home as a daughter. Ramakrishna weeping for both Kali and Krishna. And now a singer on a train platform, looking for the person of the heart. Bengal doesn't keep its streams in separate channels. They meet in songs.
screen: `THE BIRD IN THE CAGE` · `THE PERSON OF THE HEART` · `NO CASTE THE SINGER CAN SEE` · `THE STREAMS MEET IN SONGS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the bird in the cage. Sit, and let the breath slow. Feel the body: its edges, its weight on the chair, the breath moving in and out. That's the cage, and it's a good one. Now notice what's alive in it that you can't quite point to: the one who's noticing. Don't try to catch it. Just keep it company, the way you'd sit quietly near a bird so it won't fly off. If you pray, you can greet God as the person of the heart, closer than the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, the Bauls, wandering singers of the person of the heart, where Bengal's streams run together in a song. Today's word.
screen: `BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, hum one song you love, slowly, and listen for who inside you is listening. Tomorrow we walk west, to Maharashtra, and a pilgrimage on foot. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Bauls travel and sing at village fairs, on trains and at gatherings, accompanying themselves on the one-stringed ektara, and their songs, including Lalon's, are sung widely in Bengal.

notes: Editor pass: hook opener changed for variety; unsourced claims cut ('still sung across Bengal', 'Bauls have come from Hindu and Muslim families both'); the Hindu-and-Muslim point now comes from Lalon's caste song itself (keu mala keu tasbi gole: some wear a mala, some a tasbih). Confirm that line's paraphrase; Sufi influence now given as what some readers hear.
Last Bengal day in this run; the teach looks back over 1376–1381. Close points to day 1382, Maharashtra's Varkari.
Lalon's songs are paraphrased; confirm the transliterated first lines and the paraphrases (the unknown bird in the cage; 'everyone asks what Lalon's caste is').

Lalon's own religious background is disputed and deliberately not stated. Bauls with Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, and Sufi influence, are stated descriptively and without ranking. Confirm framing suits the Hindu path, since many Bauls stand outside orthodox Hinduism.
'moner manush' (the person of the heart) transliteration: confirm.
